hints: Look closely at item 3. Remember starch is not a single molecule, it is a mixture. What two polysaccharides make it up?
Recall the simple rule: 1,4 bonds make straight chains and 1,6 bonds make branch points. Which of 1 and 2 are branched storage polysaccharides?
walkthrough:
**Recall what 1,6 bonds do**

Think of alpha-glucose chains like strings of beads. The beads join end to end with 1,4 glycosidic bonds to make a straight chain.

A 1,6 bond is the side branch that sticks out to start a new chain. So only branched polysaccharides have them.

**Check amylopectin and glycogen**

Amylopectin is branched, with 1,4 bonds in the chains and 1,6 bonds at every branch point. So 1 is correct.

Glycogen is also branched, in fact even more highly branched than amylopectin, so it also has 1,4 bonds plus many 1,6 bonds at branches. So 2 is correct.

**Remember what starch really is**

This is the clever part. Starch is not one molecule. It is a mixture of two polysaccharides: unbranched amylose plus branched amylopectin.

Because starch always contains amylopectin, a sample of starch will always contain 1,6 bonds from that amylopectin part. So 3 is also correct, giving 1, 2 and 3.

options.A: Correct and well done. Amylopectin and glycogen are both branched so have 1,6 bonds, and starch contains amylopectin so it also contains 1,6 bonds.
options.B: Close but incomplete. It correctly includes amylopectin and glycogen but forgets that starch contains amylopectin and so must also contain 1,6 bonds.
options.C: Not quite. It leaves out glycogen, but glycogen is highly branched and has many 1,6 bonds at its branch points.
options.D: Not quite. It leaves out amylopectin, but amylopectin is the classic branched plant polysaccharide with 1,6 bonds at branches.
